full_judgment:
4. The accused was in jail hajat in connection with another case. He was produced before the Tribunal on 14-1-2002. In the meantime prosecution examined 4(four) witnesses. On 2-4-2002 the accused filed an application under section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure praying for recall of said 4(four) prosecution witnesses and on that date prosecution examined witness No.5 who was cross-examined. On 18-4-2002 prosecution examined witness No.6 who was cross-examined and on that date the learned Judge of the Tribunal allowed the prayer of the accused for recall of  PWs 2, 3 and 4. On 8-5-2002 PW 2 was cross examined on recall only. On that date PW 1 as Investigation Officer was examined and cross-examined and closed the evidence on behalf of the prosecution. Thereafter, the accused was examined on 8-5-2002 under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and he pleaded not guilty and declined to adduce any evidence. 

 6. The learned Judge of the trial Court after conclusion of the trial, perusing the evidence on record and hearing the arguments of the parties by his judgment and order dated 30-5-2002 convicted and sentenced the accused as stated above. 

 8. Mr Abdul Halim Mondal, the learned Advocate with Mr Kanai Lal Shah appearing for the appellant taking us through the First Information Report, charge sheet, Charge, evidence of PWs, order sheets of the case and the judgment and order under challenge submits that the appellant was falsely implicated in the case. The seizure of the alleged arms and ammunition were not held in compliance of the provision of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as local witnesses were not present at the time of alleged search and recovery. Prosecution failed to prove that the alleged place of occurrence belongs to the appellant and that did not seize and produce wood as alamat wherefrom the alleged arms were recovered. He next submits that the alleged arms and ammunition were not recovered from the exclusive possession and actual control of the appellant. He submits further that the conviction of the appellant is based on the evidence of the police witnesses which are contradictory and inconsistent and not corroborated by the seizure list witnesses. The police witnesses were partisan and they were logically interested in securing conviction and sentence of the appellant. But the learned Judge of the Tribunal missed and overlooked the improbabilities, inconsistencies and contradictions occurring in the testimonies of the police witnesses disproving the prosecution case. He, thus submits that the learned Judge of the Tribunal relying solely on the evidence of the police witnesses in the absence of corroboration by the public witness passed the impugned judgment and order convicting and sentencing the appellant is bad in law, inasmuch as unwarranted in the facts and circumstances and against the weight of evidence on record for which the same is liable to be set aside and the appellant should be acquitted. 

 9. Mr Zahirul Haque Zahir, the learned Deputy Attorney-General along with Mr Md Shafiqul Islam Siddique and Ms Sharmina Haque, Assistant Attorneys-General appearing for the respondent supporting the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence of the appellant, submits that the learned Judge of the Tribunal passed the same on the basis of cogent and reliable evidence and does not suffer from any infirmity. He also submits that the prosecution witnesses are natural and competent witnesses and, as such, the impugned judgment and order does not call for any interference by this Court. 

 10. We have heard the learned Advocates, perused the evidence on record and the impugned judgment and order convicting and sentencing the appellant. 

 11. In order to appreciate the respective arguments of the learned Advocates we now discuss the evidence adduced by the prosecution in the case. Prosecution in order to prove the case against the convict appellant produced 6 witnesses during trial. 

 24. These are all about the evidence adduced on behalf of the prosecution. We shall now scrutinise the evidence to find out whether impugned order of conviction and sentence is sustainable. 

 25. In this background of the evidence on record, the point that arises for consideration is whether the prosecution has been able to prove beyond reasonable doubt the recovery of the arms and ammunition from the exclusive possession and actual control of the accused appellant on the evidence on record. 

 26. Section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure envisages the procedure of seizure of articles. Before making a search, the searching officer is required to call two or more respectable persons of the locality in which the place to be searched is situated to attend and search shall be made in their presence and a list of articles so seized shall be prepared by such officer and signed by such witnesses. 

 27. In the instant case from the evidence of PW 1, the informant we find that he before calling the witnesses found the arms and ammunition by turning the wood stake and thereafter called two witnesses and recovered the seized arms and ammunition. From his evidence it also appears that at the time of search none was present in the place of occurrence. The seizure list witnesses PW 5 Jahangir and PW 6 Shukur Ali in their evidence stated that they were not present at the place of occurrence at the time of recovery of alleged arms and ammunition. Their signature were taken by the police in white blank paper sitting at the police station which they testified. PW 1, the informant even did not ascertain as to the ownership of the house in question, that is, the place of occurrence which was a tin shed house with jute stick (9tit v fencing wall but without any boundary wall of the premises situated in the local pourashava which means the place of occurrence was open place having access to any one. From his deposition it appears that when he went to the place of occurrence and entering into the room none was present there. Turning the wood stake in the room he found some country-made arms and then he called 2 local witnesses. It can safely be said the place of occurrence was not in exclusive possession of the convict appellant. Thus it is evident that search and seizure of the arms and ammunition was not done in compliance of the provisions of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 28. Next point to be considered is, whether the seized arms and ammunition were recovered from possession and control of the convict appellant. Possession must be exclusive and conscious and control must be actual which is essential to constitute offence. Further to constitute offence under section 19A and 19(f) of the Arms Act there must be mens rea or guilty knowledge. In the case in hand we find from the evidence that in the place of occurrence there is possibility of access of any one. 

 29. The conviction and sentence of the appellant is based on the evidence of police party, that is, PWs 1 to 4 and not corroborated by the public witnesses PWs 5 and 6. It is now well settled proposition of law that evidence of police personnel are also evidence within the meaning of section 3 of the Evidence Act, 1872. There is no reason to discard their evidence if those do not appear falsehood. An accused may be convicted on the basis of unimpeachable evidence of police personnel who made search and seizure even if not supported by the local witnesses. Our this view find support from the decision in the case of Nurul Islam vs State reported in 1988 BLD 106. 

 30. In view of the above legal position now let us see whether the seized arms and ammunitions were recovered from exclusive possession and actual control of the convict appellant. PW 1 as informant as well as Investigating Officer in his deposition stated that he went to the place of occurrence to arrest the convict appellant in connection with another case. He going there immediately on turning the wood stake kept in the room of the convict appellant found some country-made guns thereunder and at that time none was present there. But PWs 2 to 4 in their deposition stated that on showing of the mother of the convict appellant the informant recovered the seized arms and ammunition from beneath the bed of the convict appellant. So, we find there are contradictions and inconsistencies in the evidence of the PWs 1 to 4. Further before search the PW 1 did not call any local witness in compliance of provisions of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The seizure list witnesses PWs 5 and 6 in their deposition stated they did not see the recovery of the seized arms and ammunitions. They further, said that while they went to the police station for their own business the Investigating Officer took their signatures on the white paper. Further it appears that PW 6 is an inhabitant of Tambalkhana, a different area who definitely cannot be the neighbour of the place of occurrence of Alipur. So, we find discrepancies, inconsistencies and contradictions in the evidence. But the learned Judge of the Tribunal failed to notice the aforesaid contradictions and inconsistencies in the evidence of PWs 1 to 4 at least. 

 32. In view of the evidence and legal position discussed above we are of the considered view the prosecution has miserably failed to prove the offence charged under section 19A and 19(f) of the Arms Act against the convict appellant beyond all reasonable shadow of doubt and, therefore, he is not guilty of the charge. Thus the impugned judgment and order convicting and sentencing the convict appellant cannot be sustained.
